title: Unit tests with Vitest
goal: Write fast, focused unit tests for your service logic and learn the arrange-act-assert habit.

concepts: Why test: confidence to change code, documentation of behaviour
The test pyramid: many unit tests, fewer integration, few end-to-end
Vitest: describe, it/test, expect, toBe vs toEqual, toThrow / rejects.toThrow
Arrange, act, assert
Fakes: an in-memory repo implementing the same interface
vi.fn() and vi.useFakeTimers() for time-dependent code
Coverage reports (and why 100% isn't the goal)

resources.title: Martin Fowler: The practical test pyramid

build.task: In api-starter: npm i -D vitest @vitest/coverage-v8 and add scripts test and test:coverage. Write unit tests for your projects and tasks services using the in-memory repos as fakes (your interface design pays off now): creating a project, duplicate names → ConflictError, tasks for a missing project → NotFoundError, filtering, sorting and pagination meta (including the last page and an empty result), and an 'overdue' helper tested with fake timers. Aim for 20+ meaningful tests. Commit the coverage summary in docs/testing.md with notes on what is NOT tested yet.
acceptance: npm test runs 20+ passing tests in under 5 seconds
Tests use fakes, not the real database
Each error type is tested (rejects.toThrow with the class)
Pagination edge cases covered (last page, page beyond the end, empty list)
Time-based logic tested with vi.useFakeTimers / vi.setSystemTime
docs/testing.md includes the coverage summary and known gaps

hints: toBe checks identity (===); toEqual compares structure. For objects with dates or ids, use expect.objectContaining({ name: 'Website' }) or expect.any(String).
beforeEach(() => { repo = new InMemoryProjectsRepo(); service = new ProjectsService(repo); }) gives every test a fresh state, so tests can't affect each other.
proof: Commit with the tests and docs/testing.md.

explainBack.q: Why did using a repo interface make the services easy to test?
What's the difference between toBe and toEqual, with an example where they differ?

lastHintExplanation: Because services depend on a repo interface rather than on PostgreSQL, tests can pass in a fresh in-memory repo, so they run in milliseconds without a database and can't interfere with each other. toBe uses ===, so two separate objects with the same contents fail; toEqual compares contents deeply, which is what you usually want for objects and arrays.

predict.why: Two array literals are different objects; use toEqual.

dsa.note: In a BST, everything left is smaller and everything right is bigger. Use that to search in O(height).

title: API integration tests with supertest
goal: Test real HTTP requests through your Express app, including validation, errors and status codes.

concepts: Integration tests: routes + middleware + services working together
supertest: request(app).post('/api/...').send(body).expect(201)
Why createApp() without listen() makes this easy
Asserting status, headers and body shape
Injecting in-memory repos into createApp for fast HTTP tests
Testing the error format consistently

resources.title: Vitest: Test context and lifecycle hooks

build.task: In api-starter: npm i -D supertest @types/supertest. Change createApp to accept its dependencies ({ projectsRepo, tasksRepo, usersRepo }) so tests can pass in-memory repos. Write tests/api/*.test.ts covering: register (201, 400 on a weak password, 409 duplicate), login (200 with token, 401 wrong password), every projects and tasks route with a valid token (201/200/204), 401 without a token, 404 for another user's project (IDOR test), 400 for invalid query params, the list meta shape, and X-Request-Id on responses. Write a helper that registers and logs in a user and returns the token.
acceptance: createApp accepts injected dependencies
Auth, projects and tasks endpoints each have success and failure tests
An explicit IDOR test proves user B can't access user A's data
Error responses are checked for your error format
A reusable auth helper keeps tests short
npm test runs unit and API tests together

hints: const res = await request(app).post('/api/projects').set('Authorization', `Bearer ${token}`).send({ name: 'Website' }); expect(res.status).toBe(201); expect(res.body).toMatchObject({ name: 'Website' });

Helper: async function loginAs(app, email) { await request(app).post('/api/auth/register').send({ email, name: 'Test', password: 'password123' }); const r = await request(app).post('/api/auth/login').send({ email, password: 'password123' }); return r.body.token; }
Use a lower bcrypt cost in tests (e.g. read BCRYPT_COST from config, set it to 4 in test) so auth tests stay fast.

explainBack.q: What do API tests catch that your service unit tests miss?
Why test the IDOR case explicitly?
lookFor: easy to break when adding routes

lastHintExplanation: Unit tests check the service logic in isolation. API tests run the whole HTTP pipeline (routing, middleware order, validation, auth, error formatting), which is where wiring mistakes hide. An explicit IDOR test is a guard rail: a new route that forgets user_id scoping fails the build instead of reaching production.

predict.q: A supertest test calls request(app) where app is created with createApp() but never listens. Does it work?
options: Yes, supertest binds a temporary port itself
predict.why: supertest starts the app on an ephemeral port internally.

dsa.note: Pass down min and max bounds; checking only direct children is a classic mistake.

title: Testing against a real PostgreSQL database
goal: Test your Postgres repositories and SQL against a real test database, with clean data for every test.

concepts: Why fakes aren't enough: SQL typos, constraints, joins and types need a real database
A separate test database (taskmanager_test) via DATABASE_URL in .env.test
Running migrations before the test suite (globalSetup)
Resetting data between tests: TRUNCATE ... RESTART IDENTITY CASCADE
Running DB tests in a single thread to avoid clashes
Optional: Docker or Testcontainers for a throwaway Postgres

build.task: In api-starter: create taskmanager_test and .env.test. Add a Vitest project (or separate config) for tests/db/*.test.ts with a globalSetup that runs your migrations, and a beforeEach that truncates all tables. Test PostgresProjectsRepo and PostgresTasksRepo directly: create and read back, unique name per user (same name for different users is allowed), CASCADE on project delete, filters, sorting with nulls last, pagination counts, user scoping (another user's id returns nothing), and the task+tags transaction rolling back on failure. Add npm scripts test:unit, test:db and test (both).
acceptance: DB tests run against a separate test database, never the dev one
Migrations run once before the suite; tables truncated before each test
Constraint behaviour (unique, FK, CHECK, CASCADE) tested for real
User scoping tested at the SQL level
Transaction rollback test proves no partial data is left
npm run test:unit works without Postgres; npm run test:db needs it

hints: Guard against wiping the wrong database: in setup, if (!process.env.DATABASE_URL?.includes('_test')) throw new Error('Refusing to run DB tests on a non-test database');
vitest.db.config.ts: test: { include: ['tests/db/**/*.test.ts'], globalSetup: './tests/db/setup.ts', fileParallelism: false }
Force a rollback: create a task with a tag name that violates a constraint (e.g. too long or null), then assert SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tasks is still 0.
proof: Commit with DB tests and configs.

explainBack.q: Name two bugs a DB test would catch that a unit test with fakes would not.
Why must DB tests never run against your development database?

lastHintExplanation: Fakes only check that the service logic is right. They can't catch a misspelled column, a JOIN that drops rows, a $3 that should be $4, or a constraint that rejects real data; only a real database can. DB tests truncate tables before each test, so pointing them at the dev database would wipe it, which is why the setup refuses anything not named *_test.

dsa.note: In-order traversal of a BST visits values in sorted order; stop at the kth.

title: Logging, health checks and API documentation
goal: Make your API observable and self-documenting, like a production service.

concepts: Structured JSON logging with pino (levels, request id, no secrets)
pino-http for request logs; pretty output only in development
Health and readiness: /health (process up) vs /ready (database reachable)
Graceful shutdown: stop accepting requests, finish in-flight ones, close the pool
OpenAPI: a machine-readable description of your API
Swagger UI for interactive docs

resources.title: Express: Health checks and graceful shutdown

build.task: In api-starter: replace console logs with pino and pino-http (request id included, authorization header redacted, LOG_LEVEL from config, pino-pretty only in development). Add GET /health and GET /ready (runs SELECT 1; returns 503 if the database is down). Handle SIGTERM and SIGINT: stop the server, wait for requests to finish, close the pg pool, then exit. Write openapi.yaml describing auth, projects and tasks (schemas, security scheme, error format) and serve Swagger UI at /docs in development. Test /ready by stopping Postgres.
acceptance: Logs are JSON with level, time, request id; no tokens or passwords
/health always 200 while running; /ready 503 when Postgres is stopped
Ctrl+C shuts down cleanly (log shows the pool closing)
openapi.yaml covers every endpoint with request and response schemas
Swagger UI works at /docs and can call the API with a Bearer token

hints: pinoHttp({ logger, genReqId: (req, res) => res.locals.requestId, redact: ['req.headers.authorization', 'req.body.password'] }).
Shutdown: process.on('SIGTERM', () => { server.close(async () => { await pool.end(); process.exit(0); }); setTimeout(() => process.exit(1), 10_000).unref(); });

In openapi.yaml, add components.securitySchemes.bearerAuth: { type: http, scheme: bearer, bearerFormat: JWT } and security: [{ bearerAuth: [] }] on protected paths. Swagger UI then shows an Authorize button.
proof: Commit with logging, health, shutdown and openapi.yaml.

explainBack.q: What's the difference between /health and /ready, and who uses them?
lookFor: used by load balancers/orchestrators like Coolify/Docker

explainBack.q: Why log in JSON instead of plain text?

lastHintExplanation: /health answers 'is the process alive?' (if not, restart it). /ready answers 'can it serve requests right now?' (if the database is down, stop sending traffic). Platforms like Docker and Coolify use these checks. JSON logs can be filtered by fields such as requestId or level, so you can follow one failing request through thousands of log lines.

predict.q: A deploy sends SIGTERM while a request is half done. Without graceful shutdown, what happens?
options: It's cut off and the client gets an error
predict.why: The process exits immediately and in-flight requests are dropped.

dsa.note: If both values are smaller, go left; if both are bigger, go right; otherwise you're at the answer.

title: Mini project: full-stack notes with accounts
goal: Build a complete small full-stack app end to end, in one day, using everything from Phase 4.

concepts: Planning a full-stack feature: schema → API → tests → UI
Reusing your api-starter structure
Full-text search in PostgreSQL (to_tsvector, plainto_tsquery) or ILIKE
Running frontend and backend together (two terminals or npm-run-all)

build.task: Turn your angular-notes app into a full-stack app: create a new repo notes-fullstack (or a monorepo with api/ and web/). Backend: users and notes tables (title, body, tags text[], pinned, timestamps), register/login with JWT, notes CRUD scoped by user, search across title and body, and filtering by tag. At least 10 API tests including an IDOR test. Frontend: reuse your Angular notes UI, add login/register, the auth interceptor and guard, and point the store at the API. A root npm run dev starts both. README with setup steps, .env.example and screenshots.
acceptance: Register, login, and full notes CRUD work end to end
Each user only sees their own notes (tested)
Search across title and body works, plus tag filtering
10+ API tests pass
One command starts frontend and backend
README lets a stranger run the app from scratch

hints: Plan in this order: migration → repo → service → routes → API tests → Angular. Don't touch the UI until the API tests pass.
Tags as a Postgres array: tags TEXT[] NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}', and filter with WHERE $2 = ANY(tags).
Root package.json: "dev": "concurrently -n api,web \"npm --prefix api run dev\" \"npm --prefix web start\""

explainBack.q: Walk through what happens when a logged-in user creates a note, from the click to the database and back.
lookFor: requireAuth → validate → controller → service → repo INSERT with user_id

explainBack.q: Which part took longest and what would you do differently?

lastHintExplanation: Building API-first with tests means the UI connects to something you already trust. When the Angular side misbehaves, you know the bug is in the frontend. The request path is: form → store → HttpClient → auth interceptor → requireAuth → validation → controller → service → repo (scoped by user_id) → response → signal update.

dsa.note: At each node, the longest path through it is depth(left) + depth(right). Track the maximum while computing depths.

title: Phase 4 review: backend machine coding
goal: Prove Phase 4 stuck by building a small, tested, secure API from scratch under time pressure.

concepts: Phase 4 summary: Node, Express, REST, validation, PostgreSQL, auth, security, testing
Backend interview rounds: build an API in 90–120 minutes and explain your choices
Prioritise: correct schema, working endpoints, validation and auth, then tests

build.task: Timed (2 hours, no notes for the first 75 minutes): new repo 'bookmarks-api'. Users register and log in (JWT). Bookmarks: url (valid URL), title, tags, created_at; CRUD scoped by user; list with ?tag= and ?q= (search title and url) and pagination. Validation with zod, consistent errors, PostgreSQL with migrations, rate-limited auth, and at least 8 supertest tests including IDOR. Commit 'checkpoint: no notes' at 75 minutes. Then write docs/phase4-review.md: what you built unaided, what you looked up, your top 3 weak topics and a plan for each.
acceptance: 'checkpoint: no notes' commit within 75 minutes
Auth and bookmarks CRUD work, scoped by user
Filtering, search and pagination work
8+ tests pass, including an IDOR test
phase4-review.md is honest and specific

hints: First 10 minutes: write the migration and the list of endpoints with status codes. Then build auth → bookmarks → list queries → tests.
Copy patterns, not files: you've written every piece of this in the last five weeks.
If you get stuck on something for more than 10 minutes in the no-notes part, leave a TODO and move on.
proof: Links to the checkpoint commit and the final commit.

explainBack.q: Explain how a request to GET /bookmarks?tag=dev&page=2 is handled, layer by layer.
lookFor: parameterised SQL with user_id, tag, LIMIT/OFFSET

explainBack.q: Which Phase 4 topic are you least confident in, and what's your plan?

lastHintExplanation: Backend interviewers look for a sound schema, correct status codes, validation, auth with per-user scoping, parameterised SQL and a few meaningful tests, in roughly that order. Being able to explain the path of one request through every layer shows you understand the system, not just the syntax.
